present.name: Present-tense verb endings
present.about: The verb's ending changes with who does it: parlo (I speak), parli (you speak), parla (he or she speaks), parliamo (we speak).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

present.short: The verb's ending says who: bevo, bevi, beve (I drink, you drink, he or she drinks).

no-subject.name: No subject needed
no-subject.about: A verb's ending already says who, so Italian usually leaves out io, tu and the other subject words: Parlo (I speak), Piove (rains).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

no-subject.short: The verb's ending already says who, so io and tu are usually left out: Bevo caffè (drink coffee: I drink coffee).

gender.name: Gender and agreement
gender.about: Articles and adjectives match a noun's gender (la casa nuova: the house new), and so does a past form after essere or after lo, la, li or le: Lei è partita (she is gone), L'ho vista (her I-have seen).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gender.short: Every noun is an il word or a la word, and un and the adjectives with it match: il telefono, la borsa, molto caffè, molta acqua.

adjective-after.name: Adjectives after the noun
adjective-after.about: Most describing words come after the noun: una macchina rossa (a car red).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

adjective-after.short: Most adjectives come after the noun: una macchina rossa (a car red).

negation.name: non before the verb
negation.about: non goes right before the verb, and before any little pronoun in front of it: Non lo so (not it I know).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

negation.short: non goes right before the verb: Non bevo caffè (not I drink coffee: I don't drink coffee).

question.name: Questions
question.about: A yes-or-no question keeps the order of a statement, with your voice going up, and a question word comes first, often with the verb right after it: Dove abita tuo fratello (where lives your brother).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

question.short: A question keeps a statement's order, and your voice rises: Sei pronto? A question word goes first: Dov'è la macchina?

c-e.name: c'è, ci sono: there is, there are
c-e.about: c'è (there is) goes with one thing or something you don't count, ci sono (there are) with more: C'è pane (there is bread), Ci sono due bagni (there are two bathrooms).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

c-e.short: c'è says there is, ci sono there are: C'è pane (there's bread), Ci sono due bagni (there are two bathrooms).

object-pronoun.name: Object pronouns with verbs
object-pronoun.about: Little words such as mi, ti, lo, la, ci, vi, li and le normally go before a verb with a person's ending (Lo vedo: him I see), but join the end of an infinitive (vederti: see-you) or an informal command (guardalo: look-at-it).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

object-pronoun.short: lo, la, mi and ti go before the verb: Lo vedo (him I see: I see him).

piacere.name: piacere: liking
piacere.about: To like something, you say it pleases you: Mi piace il caffè (to me pleases the coffee), so the verb matches the thing you like.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

piacere.short: To like something, it pleases you: Mi piace il caffè (to me pleases the coffee: I like coffee).

reflexive.name: Reflexive and each-other verbs
reflexive.about: Some verbs use mi, ti, si, ci or vi when someone does something to themselves or people do it to each other: Mi alzo (myself I raise: I get up), Ci vediamo (each other we see: we meet).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

reflexive.short: Some verbs take mi, ti or si, pointing back to whoever does it: Mi alzo (myself I raise: I get up).

modal.name: Verb + infinitive
modal.about: After volere, potere and dovere, the next verb is in its basic form, the infinitive, with no word for to: Voglio partire (I want leave).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

modal.short: After volere, potere and dovere the next verb stays in its basic form, with no word for to: Voglio mangiare (I want eat).

perfect.name: Past events with avere
perfect.about: For most past events, use avere and the verb's past form: Ho mangiato (I have eaten), for both I ate and I have eaten.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

perfect.short: Most past events use avere and the past form: Ho mangiato (I have eaten), for I ate and I have eaten.

essere-perfect.name: Past events with essere
essere-perfect.about: Some common verbs of going, coming and staying use essere instead, and the past form's ending matches who did it: Lei è partita (she is gone: she left).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

essere-perfect.short: Verbs of going, coming and staying take essere, and the ending matches who: Lei è partita (she is gone: she left).

articulated.name: al, del, nella: preposition + the
articulated.about: a, di, da, in and su join the word for the after them: al mare (to-the sea), nella borsa (in-the bag).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

articulated.short: su, in and di run into the after them: sul tavolo (on the table), nella borsa (in the bag), della macchina (of the car).

possessive.name: Articles with possessives
possessive.about: Italian normally puts an article before mio, tuo and the rest (la mia casa: the my house), but drops it before one family member on their own (mia madre), except with loro (la loro madre).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

possessive.short: mio and mia come with the: il mio telefono, la mia chiave; but not with one family member: mia madre, mio padre.

di.name: di: of
di.about: Italian joins nouns with di where English uses 's: la macchina di mio padre (the car of my father).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

di.short: Italian joins nouns with di where English uses 's: la macchina di mio padre (the car of my father).

progressive.name: stare + -ando, -endo: right now
progressive.about: stare with a verb ending in -ando or -endo says what's happening right now: Sto mangiando (I stay eating: I'm eating).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

progressive.short: stare with a verb ending in -ando or -endo says what's happening now: Sto mangiando (I'm eating).

avere.name: avere: I have hunger
avere.about: Where English says I'm hungry or I'm twenty, Italian says I have: Ho fame (I have hunger), Ho venti anni (I have twenty years).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

avere.short: Where English says I'm hungry or I'm twenty, Italian says I have: Ho fame (I have hunger).

demonstrative.name: questo, questa: this
demonstrative.about: questo goes with an il word and questa with a la word, for this: questo libro, questa chiave. On its own, questo points at a thing: Questo è un libro (this is a book). For that, Italian says quello.

source.note: Added with the Italian lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.short: questo goes with an il word and questa with a la word, for this: questo libro, questa chiave. On its own: Questo è un libro.

lei-formal.name: Lei: polite you
lei-formal.about: Lei, often written with a capital L, is the polite you, for someone you don't know well, with the verb's lui and lei form: Lei sa dov'è? (she knows where is?: do you know where it is?)

source.note: Added with the Italian lessons, open to correction.

lei-formal.short: Lei is the polite you, with the verb's lui and lei form: Lei vuole un caffè? (she wants a coffee?: do you want a coffee?)

verb-preposition.name: A verb and its link
verb-preposition.about: Learn the link with the verb: cercare takes its object directly, without a word for for: Cerco la chiave (I look for the key). Other verbs have their own links.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

verb-preposition.short: cercare takes its object directly: Cerco la chiave. English needs for; Italian has no preposition here.

infinitive-links.name: Links before an infinitive
infinitive-links.about: An infinitive can follow a linking word. per gives a purpose: soldi per pagare (money to pay). Other constructions choose their own link, so learn the whole expression.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

infinitive-links.short: per + infinitive gives a purpose: soldi per pagare (money to pay). Learn the link with the expression.

time-telling.name: At two o'clock
time-telling.about: For an appointment or another event at two, say alle due: Ho un appuntamento alle due. alle joins a and le. Italian does not need a separate word for o'clock here.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-telling.short: alle due means at two o'clock: Ho un appuntamento alle due.

conditional.name: vorrei: I would like
conditional.about: vorrei is the conditional form of volere for io. It softens a wish or request: Vorrei un appuntamento (I would like an appointment). voglio means I want.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

conditional.short: vorrei means I would like, softer than voglio (I want): Vorrei un appuntamento.

plural.name: More than one
plural.about: A plural noun names more than one. Many nouns ending in -o change to -i: appuntamento, appuntamenti. Other endings follow other patterns; some nouns keep their form. Matching articles and adjectives must be plural too.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

plural.short: More than one appuntamento becomes appuntamenti: Ho due appuntamenti (I have two appointments).

imperative.name: Asking someone to act
imperative.about: Use a command to ask someone to do something. With tu, chiamare gives chiama: Chiama il medico (call the doctor). per favore makes the request courteous. Other verbs and other people have their own command forms.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.short: Chiama il medico, per favore: call the doctor, please. chiama is a command to someone you say tu to.

because.name: Giving a reason
because.about: perché introduces a reason or asks why. A reason can follow the main clause: Resto a letto perché voglio dormire. Italian does not send the verb to the end of the reason clause.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

because.short: perché means because in Resto a letto perché voglio dormire, and why in Perché non dormi?

partitive.name: Some and a little
partitive.about: del, della and related forms can express an unspecified amount, as in del caffè. The same forms also mean of the in other contexts. un po' di gives a small amount: un po' di acqua.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

partitive.short: del caffè means some coffee; un po' di acqua means a little water. Context distinguishes some from of the.

negative-words.name: Nobody, nothing, never
negative-words.about: After the verb, niente, nessuno and mai normally combine with non: Non compro niente. Before the verb, niente or nessuno normally supplies the negation: Nessuno viene.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

negative-words.short: Use non with niente, nessuno or mai after the verb: Non compro niente; Non bevo mai latte. Before the verb: Nessuno viene.

subjunctive.name: An opinion or a hope
subjunctive.about: In standard Italian, penso che and spero che normally take a subjunctive for a present or later situation: Penso che sia una buona idea. che alone does not determine the mood. With the same subject, an infinitive is often natural: Spero di dormire.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

subjunctive.short: After penso che or spero che, standard Italian normally uses a subjunctive: Penso che sia una buona idea; Spero che lui possa venire.

ci.name: ci: there
ci.about: ci can refer back to a known place: Ci vado, I am going there; Alle tre ci sono, I will be there at three. It is distinct from ci meaning us or to us and from existential ci sono, there are. Later, ci can also replace a complement licensed by a verb.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

ci.short: ci can replace a known place: Ci vado means I am going there; Alle tre ci sono means I will be there at three.

gli-le.name: gli and le: to him and to her
gli-le.about: gli means to him and le means to her when they are singular indirect objects. They normally precede a conjugated verb: Gli do il numero. Capital Le can be polite to you. These pronouns can also attach to infinitives and certain commands when those constructions are taught.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

gli-le.short: Gli do il numero means I give him the number; le do il numero means I give her the number. Polite Le means to you.

adverbs.name: Adverbs: almost, definitely, well
adverbs.about: Adverbs describe an action or qualify another expression and do not agree in gender or number. quasi means almost; sicuramente means definitely. Position depends on what they qualify. Many adverbs use an adjective's feminine singular form plus -mente, with spelling changes in some words; others, such as bene, have their own form.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

adverbs.short: quasi and sicuramente do not change with the person: Sono quasi pronto; Ho sicuramente bisogno di un minuto.

comparative.name: Comparing times with prima
comparative.about: prima can mean earlier or sooner than a time understood from the situation. To name the comparison, use prima di: Arrivo prima di te. A measure says how much earlier: un minuto prima. Other comparisons use their own constructions.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

comparative.short: prima means earlier in Arrivo prima di te (I arrive earlier than you) and un minuto prima (a minute earlier).

ne.name: ne with a quantity
ne.about: ne can replace a known noun when saying how many or how much: Ne ho due (I have two). It precedes a conjugated verb here. The number or amount remains; in Non ne ho, the negative means there are none in my possession. Later uses can replace other complements with di.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

ne.short: ne refers to the things counted or the substance measured: Ne ho due; Ne abbiamo abbastanza. English often leaves of them or of it unsaid.

imperfect.name: Past habits and background
imperfect.about: The imperfect describes past habits, states or ongoing background. A volte prendevamo un caffè insieme describes a repeated habit. A completed, bounded event normally uses the passato prossimo instead. English simple past can translate either, so choose from the situation.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

imperfect.short: Use the imperfect for a past habit: A volte prendevamo un caffè insieme (we sometimes had coffee together).

real-condition.name: If something happens
real-condition.about: A real condition introduced by se uses the indicative: Se hai tempo, mandami la foto. The result can be a statement or a request. The present can also describe a future possibility, and the main clause does not change its word order just because the condition comes first.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

real-condition.short: For a real possibility, use se with the indicative: Se hai tempo, mandami la foto (if you have time, send me the photo).

modal-perfect.name: Was able to, had to
modal-perfect.about: In the compound past, potere, dovere and volere take their past participle followed by an infinitive. Ho dovuto tirare means I had to pull. These examples use avere. Auxiliary choice depends on the construction and the following verb; do not assume that every compound modal takes avere.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

modal-perfect.short: Use a past participle for the modal and leave the next verb in the infinitive: Ho dovuto tirare forte (I had to pull hard).

combined-pronouns.name: It to you, to him or to her
combined-pronouns.about: Before lo, la, li, le or ne, mi, ti, ci, vi and si change to me, te, ce, ve and se. gli and le combine with these pronouns as one word: glielo means it to him or to her. Place the pair before a conjugated verb here: Te lo mando. The context identifies the people and things.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

combined-pronouns.short: ti becomes te before lo: Te lo mando (I send it to you). glielo combines it with to him or to her: Glielo puoi dare.

subjunctive-imperfect.name: As if: come se
subjunctive-imperfect.about: come se introduces an imagined comparison. For a situation simultaneous with the main verb, use the imperfect subjunctive: Parla come se abitasse in questa casa. This form can describe an imagined situation now, not only a past time. It is also used for simultaneous or later situations after past wishes and opinions.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

subjunctive-imperfect.short: Use the imperfect subjunctive after come se for an imagined simultaneous situation: Parla come se abitasse in questa casa (she talks as if she lived in this house).

future.name: The simple future
future.about: The simple future uses its own endings and sometimes an irregular stem: lavorerò, sarò, avrò. A present with a future time can also describe a plan: Domani sono a casa. The future can also express a guess about the present when the context supports that reading.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

future.short: lavorerò means I will work, sarò I will be, and avrò I will have. The present can also describe a plan: Domani sono a casa.

duration.name: An ongoing situation: da
duration.about: For a situation continuing now, use the present with da: Abito qui da due anni; Aspetto da un'ora. da introduces either the elapsed time or the starting point. A completed duration uses a past tense; fa after a duration means ago.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

duration.short: Present + da describes what is still going on: Abito qui da due anni (I've lived here for two years); Aspetto da un'ora (I've been waiting for an hour).

relative.name: The person, thing, or place described
relative.about: che connects a noun to a clause where it is the subject or direct object: il lavoro che voglio. Keep che even when English leaves out that. dove connects a place to what happens there: la città dove abito. For other roles, Italian can use a preposition with cui, introduced later.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

relative.short: Keep che in il lavoro che voglio (the job I want). For a place, use dove: la città dove abito (the city where I live).
